_comment: OIDF conformance test-plan configuration — FAPI 2.0 Security Profile (Final),
OpenID Provider, SELF-SIGNED mutual-TLS client authentication variant (X5.2).
This is the second of the two client-authentication variants X5.2 calls for.
A note on what this variant is NOT. FAPI 2.0 §5.3.1.1 permits two families of
client authentication: private_key_jwt (RFC 7523) and mutual TLS (RFC 8705).
RFC 8705 itself defines two mTLS methods — PKI (`tls_client_auth`) and
self-signed (`self_signed_tls_client_auth`) — and this plan exercises the
second while the sibling plan exercises the first.
So the pair covers BOTH mTLS methods, not both FAPI client-auth families.
private_key_jwt is not implemented in AXIAM (X5.1's table lists it as the
second half of that row, deliberately not landed in this pass). Any
submission claiming full FAPI 2.0 client-authentication coverage needs it.
The runbook's 'Known gaps' section states this, and it is the single most
important thing to read before treating a green run here as submission-ready.
Placeholders are substituted by conformance/scripts/render-plan.sh.
W9 correction, found by the first run that ever submitted this plan to the
suite. The variant block carried `fapi_client_type`, which the suite
rejects outright:
Unknown variant parameter(s) [fapi_client_type] for plan
'fapi2-security-profile-final-test-plan'
so NO plan could be created from any of these three templates, and no FAPI
module has ever run from them. `fapi_client_type` is a FAPI 1.0 variant;
FAPI 2.0 expresses the same choice as `openid`, which these templates were
already setting to the same value, so removing it loses nothing.
`fapi_profile` is stated explicitly rather than left to default, because a
certification result should say which profile it certifies.
And a second correction from the same run: `fapi_request_method` and
`fapi_response_mode` were removed as well. They are MODULE-level variants
that the plan fixes for each of its own modules, so supplying them here is
not merely redundant — the suite refuses the whole plan:
Variant 'fapi_request_method' has been set by user, but test plan
already sets this variant for module
'fapi2-security-profile-final-discovery-end-point-verification'
The paragraph above about `pushed` still describes what happens; it is the
plan that arranges it, not this file.
W9, third correction from the first run. The discovery URL carried
`?tenant_id=${AXIAM_TENANT_ID}` and the suite failed the very first module:
CheckOauthDiscEndpointIssuer: issuer listed in the discovery document is
not consistent with the location the discovery document was retrieved
from. These must match to prevent impersonation attacks.
OIDC Discovery §4.1 ties the retrieval location to the `issuer` claim, and
a query parameter breaks that correspondence. W7 made the document
tenant-aware through exactly such a parameter, so a tenant-scoped discovery
URL cannot be a conformance plan's discoveryUrl. The FAPI lane loses
nothing by dropping it — it requests only `openid`, and the parameter's
sole effect is to advertise the `address` and `phone` scopes. What it costs
the BASIC lane is recorded in docs/conformance/ and in the plan's §4.10.
description: AXIAM — FAPI 2.0 Security Profile (Final), self-signed mTLS client auth + mTLS sender-constraining
_browser_comment: There is deliberately NO `browser` automation block here, and this is the
one place in the harness where the right answer is to do less.
The suite's built-in WebRunner is HtmlUnit. Pointed at AXIAM's /login it
fetched the document and stopped: the page it recorded is the bare Vite
index.html with a <script type=module> in it, and every element the
automation was told to fill (`org-slug`, `username`) belongs to a React
tree HtmlUnit never built. `wait id org-slug 15` therefore timed out, and
a failed browser task INTERRUPTS the module — strictly worse than no block
at all, which merely leaves it WAITING with a URL for somebody to visit.
So the visit is done by a real browser instead:
GET /api/runner/browser/<testId> for URLs the suite is waiting on and
drives them in Chromium. Run it beside `conformance-run`; see
This is a statement about the SUITE, not about AXIAM: a JavaScript sign-in
page is what a modern OP has, and the OpenID Foundation expects the
interactive hops of a certification run to be completed in a browser.
